The significant variations in the size of the human appendix among individuals challenge
the notion that it is a completely vestigial organ. If the appendix were entirely
redundant, one would expect it to be uniformly small or absent across the population;
however, its considerable size differences suggest that it may still serve a functional
purpose. Research indicates that the appendix might play a role in gut flora maintenance
and immune function, particularly in young individuals. This variability implies that the
organ may have adapted to various dietary and environmental conditions, pointing to a more
complex evolutionary history than the vestigial model suggests. Consequently, the size of
the appendix serves as evidence against the idea of its complete redundancy in human
physiology.
